translation: ...another, that of the moist and cold, and a third besides these, the dry and cold, another of the dry together with hot. Some of them say that there exists a certain moist and at the same time cold mixture, and another hot and at the same time dry, but not the moist together with hot, nor the cold together with dry; for it is not possible, they say, either for moisture to run together with a prevailing heat or for dryness with cold: for the moisture is consumed by the heat when it prevails, and so the body becomes hot and at the same time dry, while it remains unconcocted and unworked in those bodies in which the heat is weak; so that it is necessary that when heat predominates dryness follows, and when cold prevails moisture follows. These men, then, have persuaded themselves by such arguments that all the [mixtures] are two...

Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus, have stated precisely to what one must look in supposing a nature to be well-mixed or ill-mixed. But these men do not even know this; rather, when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and hot, or that the mixture of the child is moist and hot, they neither understand how these things are said, and they foolishly transfer the statement to the seasons, as though it were the same thing, and not far different, for one's own mixture to be moist and hot or that of the air surrounding us; for it is not the same thing, nor is the mixture of an animal said to be moist and hot in the same way as the mixture of air is said to be moist and hot. What the cause of all these things was I shall now relate, and I shall show clearly to those willing to pay attention how small errors among the...

...left-handed, there is nothing absurd. So too, then, a dog is moist and at the same time dry, and hot and at the same time cold, but not in relation to the same thing: in relation to a man it is dry, but moist in relation to an ant; and in relation to a man hot, but cold in relation to a lion. And indeed it is hot as a living thing, for if anything has died it is not hot; but not hot in relation to another dog, if it so happens. All these things, then, are said in relation to one another by comparison; but things said as within the genus of animals are said in another way, as again also according to the species of animal. For a dog, in relation to an ant and a bee, is moist, but as within the genus of animals, dry; and of dogs themselves according to species, this one is dry, that one moist, and some other one, as...

...of its nature is judged to be in the best state by its activities. For indeed we say that any plant or animal whatsoever is in the best condition at the time when it functions most excellently: for the excellence of a fig-tree is to bring to maturity the best and most figs, and in the same way that of the vine is to bear the most and finest grapes, that of a horse to run most swiftly, and that of a dog to be supremely spirited for hunting and guarding, but most gentle towards its own household. All these, then, I mean both animals and plants, we shall say have the best and median mixture within their own genus, not simply when there is an exact equality of the opposites, but when the proportion of it according to capacity obtains. And we say that justice too is something of such a kind: equality not by weight and measure, but by what is fitting...

For if he asked, as of a thing among animals, of what mixture it was, one must make the answer itself looking to the mean of all animals in respect of mixture; but if simply and as in relation to all substance, then one must now compare the opposites within it with one another, and consider the mixture no longer by reference to the activities but to the bulks of the elements. And if he put the question comparing it determinately with some particular thing, one must compare it with that alone; and still more, if we were asked about one of the individual substances, as for instance Dion or this particular dog, what sort its mixture is, one must not answer simply; for from here there is no small starting-point for the sophists for quibbling. For if you were to say that Dion is of a hot and dry mixture, it is very easy for him, bringing forward one of those drier and hotter than he, the...

...those of animals and those of plants and those of all inanimate things, such as bronze and iron and stones and timbers, are ranked in the interval between those primary ones. For none of them is extremely hot or extremely cold or extremely moist or extremely dry, but either it is exactly in the middle of the opposites, so as to be no more hot than cold or dry than moist, or it has moved toward one of the extremes, so as to be more hot than cold or more moist than dry. If, then, it should be exactly in the middle in respect of each of the oppositions, so as to be no more hot than cold or dry than moist, this will be called well-mixed simply; but when one has gained the advantage, either in one antithesis or in both, it is no longer well-mixed. If, then,...

...the other antithesis, the soft sinew is no longer midway between hot and cold, but falls short of heat by as much as it does of blood. And so too all the other things mentioned before are colder than skin by as much as they are more bloodless; and the coats themselves of the most blood-filled vessels, I mean of artery and vein, are bloodless and cold by nature, but by proximity to the blood they are warmed and arrive at a median state of mixture. The blood in turn has its warmth from the heart; for by nature that viscus is of all the parts of the animal at once the most blood-filled and the hottest, and next after it the liver. But the heart falls a little short of skin in hardness, the liver by much; and accordingly it is moister than skin by as much as it is softer. And indeed also...

...and in the movements of the limbs; he is of good colour and always breathes well, and is midway between sleepy and sleepless, between bare of hair and shaggy, between black in colour and white; and he has hair, as a child, rather reddish than dark, but in his prime the reverse. And since we have also made mention of the difference in him according to the ages, it would be no worse now to say something about these too. I wished, then, first to go through the causes of each of the signs mentioned; but since the inquiry concerning the ages is more pressing for the matters at hand, and renders us best furnished for the discovery of the causes, we shall now enter upon this. Let us conceive, then, the animal just being formed in the wombs of those who give birth, so that we may learn how it is moistest and hottest. For the first constitution is from...

...the nurses of infants mould the limbs as if they were of wax: so great a moisture is there in the whole body of children. But also if you take a young sacrificial animal, whether you wish to eat it or to cut it open and examine it, you will find the flesh mucous and flabby, and the whole bony kind resembling cheese that is just curdling, so that the bodies of newborn animals are not even pleasant to eat on account of their excessive moisture; and this is especially the case with swine and sheep, because they are also especially moister, while goats, because they are drier, are both better and more pleasant to eat. Conversely to the young victims, those that have grown old have all the bones and all their ligaments quite dry and sapless and juiceless, and the flesh sinewy and hard, and the arteries and the...

...a quantity of saliva collects in the mouth; but they also cough and spit up phlegm, showing thereby that the lung too is full of such a humour; and their stomach is filled with phlegm, and each of the joints is somewhat mucous. But none of these things is contrary to the bodies of the aged being dry. For you will find the sinews and the arteries and the veins and the membranes and the coats of all the organs much drier than before, but with some phlegmatic humour or mucous moisture plastered around them both inside and outside. But so far are all such signs from showing old age to be moist, that they seem to me even to bear witness to its dryness; for it is on account of this very thing that each of the parts becomes drier, that it is no longer nourished in the same way, now through weakness of the heat, a quantity...

...it seems to me, since the type of the arguments which we have stated is now clearly understood. For both parties reason from afar, and almost infer the prior things from the secondary ones; and they make their discourse as though their hearers already knew how growth, how digestion, how nutrition comes about; and likewise they go through sensation and motion and the practical and natural activities, and they mention the generation of sleep and the nature of foods, none of which is simply and easily known, but each requires a very great deal of inquiry, and perhaps cannot even be discovered unless one first knew how to recognise a moist and a dry and a hot and a cold mixture. For whatever of those things they say as though already knowing it, if one were to compel them to demonstrate it, they will in every case need the account of mixtures which is now before us; so that through one another and...

...the present discourse must not take its proofs from things not yet known; but, as is right and just, what is to be taken for the demonstration ought to be either one of the evident things or one of the things previously demonstrated. Neither, then, must the generation of sleep be mentioned, nor digestion, nor growth, nor any other of such things; but let the inquiry proceed from the mere and bare substance of the things under consideration, just as we did also throughout the first discourse. For having distinguished that what is in actuality is one thing and what is in potentiality another, we said that one must first make the discourse about what is already hot and cold and dry and moist in actuality, and then in this way come to the things in potentiality. And ready to hand for all and familiar is the [knowledge] of things already hot in actuality...

...positing [these as] principles and elements, to have strayed so far from the men who posited these things as not to know both that the principles of every demonstration are the things evident to sense-perception and to thought, and that whoever is in doubt about these inquires in vain about the rest, having left himself no starting-point. Whence, then, they turned to so long a wandering and attempted to seek by reasoning the discernment of perceptible things, I for my part cannot even conceive; and for this reason I judge by touch what is hot in actuality, while whatever is not yet hot but is fitted to become such, which indeed is also called hot in potentiality, this I try to discover by reasoning. But with them, I know not how, everything has been overturned, and long rhetoric has been practised about the arguments. These men, then, let us leave, having reminded ourselves of this much even now, that...

...nor is it reasonable at all to confirm the prior things from the later. Let us judge by sense-perception, then, the hot and the cold body, that which is already such in actuality and no longer in potentiality, leaving aside the first judgement and all the other signs. And so I release you to the test, as one who will judge well, while I myself shall set forth my own judgement. For touching carefully many bodies in succession, not of children only or of infants but also of youths and of those in their prime, I found that neither party was speaking truly, neither those who said simply that the man in his prime is hotter than the child nor those who said he is colder. For if, removing all the other alterations from outside, you were to examine the differences arising from age alone, neither appears to you hotter simply; for their heats differ in quality, owing to the unequal transpiration, through which also...

...spinal [marrow] is of the [same] kind, while all the other marrows are of another nature. The brain is moister and hotter than the spinal marrow, and for this reason also softer; and indeed of the brain itself the anterior parts are moister by just so much as they are also softer. All these, however, are not only moister than skin but also colder; and in general everything bloodless is colder than what contains blood. Closest to skin is also the nature of the soft nerves, while that of the hard ones is just like the skin itself in respect of moisture, clearly, and dryness; for in heat it falls short by as much as it is reasonable for a wholly bloodless thing to fall short of a blood-containing body. The flesh of the spleen and of the kidneys and of the liver is moister than skin by as much as it is also softer, and hotter by as much as it is also fuller of blood; and indeed the flesh of the heart too...

...catarrhs and coughs and running colds and a quantity of saliva; for all these show him to be colder and moister, and still more so if on chance occasions he falls into such conditions. Baldness, however, follows upon dryness, and the growth of black and abundant hair is a sign of good mixture of the brain. In this manner, then, one must always consider the mixture, examining each part separately, and not venture to pronounce about all from one, as some have done, saying that the snub-nosed are moist and the hook-nosed dry, and those whose eyes are small dry, those whose eyes are large moist. On this point, indeed, they have even disagreed among themselves; for some, having assumed that the eyes belong among the moist parts, in those in whom they find them larger [infer] moisture of mixture in...

...the same thing, either to evacuate some moisture scattered in certain regions, or to render the proper mixture drier. For in the inflamed parts there arises a certain uneven ill-mixture, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their proper nature but still being changed and altered, while all the intervening spaces are filled with the flux. All things, then, that are hot and moist in mixture, when applied to parts so disposed, evacuate that superfluity which has occupied the spaces between the homoeomerous bodies, but are so far from drying the bodies themselves that they even impart moisture to them. The truth, then, stands thus; but what has been said requires a demonstration which, considering it both to be longer than can be added within this discourse and further to require a hearer versed in the power of drugs, I defer, at least...

...if you wish, the yellow bile, while all the rest are hot by accident, through partaking of these: will it not then be necessary that the animal becomes hotter in two ways, either by acquiring more hot humours or by having them hotter than before? To me, at least, it appears quite so. And in the same way, I think, it will also become colder in two ways, either by the cold humours, such as phlegm and black bile, being bred in greater quantity, or by the quality alone being changed while the proportion of all of them remains. What wonder, then, if so long as food cold by nature, such as purslane and lettuce, is being digested, the body is filled with a cold quality, but when they have been thoroughly digested and have become good blood, the body becomes hotter again than itself by the generation of the hot humour? And indeed...

...the condition, if simple and single; but by time the judgement is distinguished as follows: that which, together with being applied, is manifestly seen to cool or to heat would be such, surely, both in itself and through itself; but that which does so over time might perhaps be brought to this from some accident, as in tetanus, in midsummer, in a young well-fleshed man, a pouring-over of much cold water produces a recall of heat. But that the cold water does not heat in itself is clear from the first contact: for it produces a sensation of cooling, and indeed it cools the skin so long as it is poured over it, and it furnishes the warmth neither in all bodies nor during the pouring, but only in well-fleshed young men in midsummer after the pouring has ceased. Just as, then, for those upon whom falls...

...of the well-being and benefit, of necessity this is cold, even if at times in other cases it appears hot; for it will be found, when examined precisely in those cases, not heating in itself but by some accident. And when we say 'in itself' or 'primarily' or 'through none of the intermediates', the same thing is signified in effect by all these expressions; and we shall carry out the exercise of all these together with their proper examples in the treatises on drugs. But now, having recalled again what I said also before, I shall try to put upon the present discourse its fitting conclusion. For since 'the hot body' was said in many senses (for there is both that which has the extreme quality, the element itself, and that which is so named by predominance of it, and further that which is said relative to another, either to the well-proportioned thing of the same genus or to anything whatever)...

...indeed, and with rose cerate it helps greatly for those things; for which, and for such conditions, many other drugs too will be described in the following discourse, some having a power similar to the date-plaster, some even more efficacious. But for rheumatic affections this is the best drug of all, and has often accomplished something greater than hope. When once, then, a thigh had suppurated near the groin, the inflammation throughout the whole of it being unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors flowed out toward the groin through the ulcer that had formed; and when this took a longer time, the flux that had settled into the thigh was evacuated, but a fistulous condition arose under the skin throughout the whole thigh, so that I wished to divide it near the kneecap, in order that from both sides there might be an outflow for the ichors...

...having taken in addition vinegar. For that one is useful at every season, while the white one made with pepper is useful for excoriated burns when they are being brought to a scar; before that it is useless by itself, but when dissolved in myrtle oil it is useful, though not with equal strength to the drugs that are properly suited for burns. Heras says that it is also suited for bites; but here too there is need of a distinction: for in hard and hard-to-concoct cases the drug is too weak, while in the more moderate ones it is sufficient, and especially in old men and children and women and, to speak summarily, in the soft-fleshed. The drug is also useful for pimples, as Heras wrote this too, speaking truly; but he pronounced without distinction about eruptions: for of these too it cures those that are moderately hardish, but those...

...but the measure is not equal to the Roman; for different people use different measures for the xestes. Among the Romans, at any rate, the xestes holds one litra and a half and a sixth, so that the ounces in all are 20, which for the most part they measure with horns marked off on the outside by certain circular lines. Some, however, have falsely supposed that the Roman xestes holds eighteen metrical ounces. It seems, then, that Heras too, when he writes 'kotyle', means half the xestes; but whether they indicate the 9 ounces from the litra-horn or the ten, this is unclear. And whether the drug is also suitable for those bitten by mad dogs, whether swallowed or applied externally, it is not possible to know from reasoning; for it has been shown by us that such drugs have their action by the whole peculiarity of their substance...

...about nourishment, that the bad and the not-bad is said as among relative terms, and clearly also the harmful and the beneficial. For in another respect you would say that the Attalic [plaster] is better than this plaster, in that it is more widely useful; and indeed Asclepiades himself, writing next after this one now mentioned that very one made with white pepper, does not call it Attalic but Pamphilian, being ignorant, as I think, of the man who first discovered it, and having added the name of the man who used it and gave it to him. Its promise, at any rate, he wrote word for word thus: 'Another, called Pamphilian, a well-tried drug: it works for old and hard-to-heal [ulcers], carbuncles, epinyctides, scabby achores, conditions; it glues together sinuses; it works for abscesses, condylomata', and the drug is almost more widely useful. He says it is composed of white lead...

...let each of these be [done] precisely for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. About the white lead, too, it has been said before, and about the oil and the manner of the boiling and the surrounding air and the fire, how each of them may contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the other cases, so in these too one who knows the powers of water and vinegar and sea-water and the whitest wine must mix into the composition what is most useful for the condition being treated. For in the case of ulcers with raised edges, having their lips thick and hard and needing much thinning, the [drugs] triturated with vinegar and sea-water are more useful than those with water; while in those in which the fluid carried in the ulcers is acrid and biting, one should rather triturate in water...

...each of the metallic substances, just as, conversely, in wine rather, in those cases in which the fluid flowing onto the ulcers appears abundant. Each of these, then, which I mentioned, triturated in each of the fluids named for several days, I put in on each occasion into all the drugs made with white lead and litharge, and found them all cicatrising most excellently; and I also gave some recipes to friends who were in need of such drugs, by whom too, when brought to the test, they appeared to preserve their promise. When the litharge, then, has been boiled beforehand as has been said, with the white lead, and the drug has come close to a non-staining consistency, one must add the larch resin or the terebinth resin together with the white wax, and when these have been well united, add the metallic substances, having the following proportion: of litharge and white lead, according to the usual practice, a litra of each with two litrae of oil, let it be boiled repeatedly...

...but if some scirrhous remnant of its inflammation should be left behind, to apply some of the things that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something appeared to be lacking to the drug made with the root of dragon-arum, which I had used earlier (which has all else the same as the Egyptian drug called Isis, but has taken in addition the root of dragon-arum), next after this, having used the one called Athena, from that I went on in turn to the cicatrising [drugs]. In another case, smearing the bared parts of the wound with the troche made with boiled-down must, dissolved, I applied from outside the euphorbium, having mixed it with wax and resin in such quantity as both to become plaster-like and to preserve the power of the euphorbium. How one, looking to these aims, might compose the drug, I shall say next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar...

...just as with the resin and the pitch; for this reason I mix into the cerate resin or pitch or a part of each. It is clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them: for wax needs much of the oily matter for moistness, whereas the resins, the dry ones, need altogether little, while the moist ones even want to take in some dry substance in addition for a plaster-like consistency. Among the waxes, then, the difference in respect of moisture and dryness is not great, but among the resins, conversely, as also with pitch, the difference between the dry and the moist ones is very great. The driest of the resins, then, is that which some call fried [resin], some colophony; second is that from the potteries, impure and unfried; but if one purifies it...

...to me of the operation, some, mixing up the same thing, of those inexperienced in the anatomy of all the muscles, flay off the underlying membranes, not knowing that these may be sewn together with the muscles without danger, but most dangerously the tendons that have been flattened out like them. Yet however much they themselves may be flattened, they are nonetheless still thicker than the membranes and harder. You will see tendons that are quite thin also in all the muscles of the epigastrium except the two straight ones, upon which the membranous aponeuroses of the oblique ones are laid; but no other tendon beside those mentioned is flattened out membranously, for all those that are flattened preserve a sufficient thickness so as to escape no one. Yet the sympathy of the overlying parts as far as the very origin of the nerves is no less for the muscles at the end of the thigh and for those entering the elbow of the forearm and for those...

...you have seen me doing continually, not in this case only but also with ammoniac incense. There is also the drug written after this by the Tarentine, of the same promise, in the following proportion: of chalcitis 25 drachms, of cadmia 12 drachms; having ground them separately and mixed them, pour on unadulterated wine, boiled, so that they are moderately kneaded, then grind until it is dried; and having melted wax 50 drachms, terebinth resin 30 drachms, myrtle oil 8 kotylai, mix into the cerate 20 drachms of the dry ingredients. And this drug has nothing of the emollient kind; yet in the mixture with the cerate, the fitting quantity of the admixture for each of the ulcers he who has been rationally trained in the methods I have laid down would work out suitably. And rightly also [he writes] 'unadulterated wine', that is, that with which sea-water has not been mixed...

...the meltable ingredients, having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ones onto them, stirring carefully. One must have, ground with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax; and into these is put what is in the dish, and it is ground so that lumps of wax do not form; and when it is in good state, take it up into a wooden box smeared beforehand with iris oil. On the third kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote word for word these things: 'For ulcers that do not close at all, or that close but are dissolved again, either the flesh being corrupted or the underlying bones too being corrupted, one must use the following preparations. For cheironian and hard-to-heal [ulcers], a well-tried drug: of flakes of copper, of scraped verdigris, each 1 ounce, of wax half a litra, of larch resin 1 ounce and a half; the meltable ingredients onto the dry ones, and having taken it up, use it, kneading carefully and applying a small flat piece over...'

...the metallic substances with vinegar, and after these adding the dry ingredients and grinding again; then, when these have a clay-like consistency, mixing in the meltable ingredients as has been said before. Another: of asphalt and terebinth resin and Bruttian pitch, each 1 litra; of oil 24 drachms; of litharge and white lead and manna and verdigris and flakes and opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachms of the oil; of ladanum two ounces, which is 16 drachms; and two kotylai of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another: of chrysocolla and flakes and steel, each 4 drachms; of verdigris and chalcanthum, the half of each, that is, 2 drachms each; of wax 25 drachms, that is 3 ounces and one drachm; of terebinth resin 2 ounces, that is 16 drachms. Melt the wax with the terebinth...

...it checks haemorrhoids and works excellently for affections about the bladder. It contains: of frankincense 4 drachms, of myrrh 4 drachms, of saffron 4 drachms, of Illyrian iris 4 drachms, of bdellium 4 drachms, of flakes 12 drachms, of chalcanthum 4 drachms, of split alum 4 drachms, of round [alum] 4 drachms, of ammoniac incense 4 drachms, of misy 4 drachms, of rinds of sweet pomegranate 4 drachms, of birthwort, of unripe oak-gall, each 8 drachms (otherwise 16), of chalcitis 4 drachms, of ammoniac incense 4 drachms, of oak mistletoe 8 drachms, of opopanax 8 drachms, of scraped verdigris 8 drachms, of acacia 8 drachms, of rose blossom 8 drachms, of terebinth 1 mina (others: 50 drachms), of poppy juice 6 drachms, of wax 2 minae (others: 4 drachms), of calf suet, prepared, 1 mina (others: 150), of common vinegar 2 kotylai; of wine for the dry ingredients, these...

Of verdigris of copper and of Indian aloes, of burnt copper and of good diphryges, sixteen and a half from each ingredient; twenty drachms of galbanum and four; of manna of frankincense equal amounts, twice 12; of ammoniac twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachms of Attic propolis; of long birthwort twice 10 drachms; twice 6 drachms of flakes of Cyprian copper; and of the driest root of gentian an equal amount. To all these add in addition of dittany herb, dry, having its flower, 20 holkai, ground fine. Put litharge with oil into a new earthenware wide-mouthed dish; boil over a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it acquires the thickness of Attic honey; and adding again an equal amount of the flakes, boil more fiercely; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and diphryges, making the drug non-staining and set; add the wax and the...

...of iris; but in place of molybdaena put in two parts of litharge, and of the rest one part each. A dry septic [drug] of Lecanius Areius: of arsenic 1 litra, of quicklime 2 drachms; grind in water for 30 days, changing the water twice a day, in the sun; then, having dried it out, use it. A sitz-bath for haemorrhoids, that of Phanias: of chalcanthum, of split alum, of chalcitis, of raw misy, of sandarach, each 4 drachms; have them all finely ground. At the time of use, take old salted urine of a single man, by measure 2 xestai; put it into an earthenware basin, and of the drug 12 drachms; pour in urine in addition so that the two xestai are always kept up. Use this, sitting in it, for 7 days; for in these it acts. And when it becomes gluey, smear the anus with the sediment. A dry [drug], cicatrising flesh, non-biting, according to Harpocras: of sandarach, of chrysocolla, of arsenic, an equal amount of each...

...of wax, nor having any other of these, but with the ammoniac incense alone put in, will render the drug parched. But for plaster-making (for it is no worse to name it so) both the wax and the resin are useful; for indeed the softening and the dispersing belong to the drug from the ammoniac alone, which holds first place among the emollients and is a rival also to the dispersives. Recalling, then, what was said in the fifth [book] of the Powers of Simple Drugs, as to what sort of mixture such drugs must have, you will need no further teaching. For the primary powers that are active in drugs are in heat and cold and moisture and dryness; and the second are the emollient and dispersive and repellent and attractive and concoctive and cleansing and septic, just as also...

...of all; carefully drip off a little again; when you see it well-coloured and well-blended, lift the pot at once from the fire and add galbanum, softened beforehand. And if the drug should be much too hard, add oil to it for good blending; thus having strained it, then into another vessel, cold, knead it with the hands and so store it away. Another I shall write out below, of the same kind as the one before this; it works for the affections I mentioned before; this one cicatrises better than all drugs ulcers hard to heal and callous and chronic; the eruptions arising on the face this one cures without any harmful biting; and seats that have fissures and hardnesses, the condylomatous ones, and calluses it casts off. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge (a mina is a litra and a third part of a litra), of good Pontic wax half a mina, of verdigris a fourth part of a mina, good scraped...

...scrofulous swellings, reducing every swelling and curing the watery conditions of the liver and of the spleen, bringing on copious excretions of urine; it loosens too the sciaticas that have become chronic. Using this, Ulpianus, a gifted young man, benefited very many. It contains one litra of Pontic wax, one of fried [resin] and one of pine resin, of fresh quicklime 1 ounce, of split alum 1 ounce, and equal to one of these, of Pontic arsenic. Having poured a little fragrant vinegar over these, grind them for a sufficient time in a larger mortar; having added to the wax and the resin a little oil, melt them over a fire of fierce flame, and mixing all carefully and making malagmata, have it stored away with the thickness of a non-staining [plaster], using it where needed with a fresh compress. And the Most Excellent, the father of the drug, used to say also for deliverances from long diseases...

...which also cure small inflammations. Of the compound emollients, some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first rank; some not much stronger than these, in the second; some in the third; others besides these in the fourth. One should use them, as has been said before, for slight hardnesses and soft bodies those of the first rank, and for bodies and affections stronger than these those of the second, just as also those of the third and the fourth in proportion. They also write out below those under each of them separately. Menecrates did this because it often happens that errors are made in the recipes not only unwillingly but also through envy, some doing so willingly: making the letter o into θ by another transverse line drawn through the middle of the round line, and the letter iota by the addition likewise of another transverse one, just as also, when one stroke has been scraped away from the letter gamma and from rho, it happens that the character of iota is left behind. And in the same manner, out of many letters, by addition of some, by combination of others, by subtraction of others, it happens that the alteration of the characters signifying them takes place. But Menecrates accomplished nothing more for the time thereafter, since those who copied his book did not write the names of the numbers out in full letters but by the characters signifying them.
